families.stem: Find the range of the set of values: ${=v[0]}, {=v[1]}, {=v[2]}, {=v[3]}, {=v[4]}, {=v[5]}$.
solution: The greatest value is ${=max(v)}$ and the smallest value is ${=min(v)}$.
families.notes: Modelled on the worked example (range = greatest - smallest). Values are distinct, unordered.

families.context: Two sets A and B of five wages, in LE, are given.
families.stem: The wages (in LE) of five workers in two sets are: Set A: ${=m - a1}, {=m - b1}, {=m}, {=m + b1}, {=m + a1}$; Set B: ${=m - a2}, {=m - b2}, {=m}, {=m + b2}, {=m + a2}$. Both sets have mean ${=m}$. Which statement is correct?
solution: The means are equal, so we compare the ranges: the larger range means the more dispersed set.
Set {=big} has the greater range, so it is more dispersed.

choices.correct: Set {=big} is more dispersed, because its range is greater

distractors.text: Set {=small} is more dispersed, because its range is greater
The sets are equally spread, because their means are equal
Set {=big} is less dispersed, because its range is greater

families.notes: Equal means by symmetric construction. The last distractor is contradictory in logic but names a plausible reversed reading; ranges are never equal because c >= a+20.

params.require: x >= 1 and x <= 120 and x not in v
params.why: fifth value positive, reasonable and distinct

families.stem: A set of five values has mean ${=M}$. Four of the values are ${=v[0]}, {=v[1]}, {=v[2]}, {=v[3]}$. Find the range of the set.
solution: Total of the four known values $= {=sum(v)}$.
families.notes: Uses mean = total / number, then range.

params.name: vals
params.let: [m + d * t for t in pat]

families.stem: Calculate the standard deviation of the values: ${=vals[0]}, {=vals[1]}, {=vals[2]}, {=vals[3]}$
solution: The deviations $x-\bar{x}$ are ${=vals[0]-m}, {=vals[1]-m}, {=vals[2]-m}, {=vals[3]-m}$, and their squares are ${=d*d}, {=d*d}, {=d*d}, {=d*d}$, so $\sum (x-\bar{x})^2={=4*d*d}$
families.notes: Symmetric data, integer mean and integer answer. Population formula (divide by n) as in the book.

params.why: mean must be a whole number

params.name: ss
params.let: sum([(x - m) ** 2 for x in vs])

families.stem: Calculate the standard deviation of the values: ${=vs[0]}, {=vs[1]}, {=vs[2]}, {=vs[3]}, {=vs[4]}$. Round your answer to 2 decimal places.
families.notes: Mirrors the book example: five distinct values with whole-number mean, answer rounded to 2 d.p.

params.require: x5 >= 1 and x5 <= 60 and x5 not in k
params.why: missing value must be positive and new

params.name: ss
params.let: sum([(x - m) ** 2 for x in all])

families.stem: Four of five values are ${=k[0]}, {=k[1]}, {=k[2]}, {=k[3]}$ and the fifth value is unknown. The mean of the five values is ${=m}$. Find the fifth value, then calculate the standard deviation of the five values. Round the standard deviation to 2 decimal places and give only the standard deviation.
solution: Since $\bar{x}=\dfrac{\sum x}{n}$, the total of the five values is $5\times {=m}={=5*m}$
The four known values total ${=sk}$, so the fifth value is ${=5*m}-{=sk}={=x5}$
The values are ${=all[0]}, {=all[1]}, {=all[2]}, {=all[3]}, {=all[4]}$ with squared deviations from ${=m}$: ${=(all[0]-m)**2}, {=(all[1]-m)**2}, {=(all[2]-m)**2}, {=(all[3]-m)**2}, {=(all[4]-m)**2}$
families.notes: Twist: find the missing value from the given mean, then compute sigma (population formula).

families.stem: A frequency distribution has the values $x$ = {=c}, {=2*c}, {=3*c}, {=4*c}, {=5*c}, which occur with frequencies $k$ = {=f[0]}, {=f[1]}, {=f[2]}, {=f[3]}, {=f[4]} respectively. Find the mean $\bar{x}$ of this distribution.
families.notes: All datasets have mean 3c (integer). Answer is whole number.

families.context: Defective units found in boxes of manufactured units.
families.stem: The frequency distribution shows the number of defective units ($x$) found in some boxes of manufactured units and the number of boxes ($k$): $x$ = {=m-d}, {=m}, {=m+d} with $k$ = {=a}, {=b}, {=a} boxes respectively. Find the standard deviation of the number of defective units.
families.notes: Datasets chosen so variance is a perfect square; sigma whole number.

families.context: Marks of students in an exam, grouped in sets of equal width.
families.stem: The frequency distribution shows the marks of {=n} students in an exam. Sets (marks): {=s0}–{=s0+w}, {=s0+w}–{=s0+2*w}, {=s0+2*w}–{=s0+3*w}, {=s0+3*w}–{=s0+4*w}, {=s0+4*w}–{=s0+5*w} with frequencies {=a}, {=b}, {=c}, {=b}, {=a} respectively. Using the centres of the sets, find the standard deviation of the marks.
solution: $\sum k = {=n}$ and, by symmetry of the frequencies, the mean $\bar{x}$ equals the middle centre {=mu}.
families.notes: Frequencies (a,b,6a,b,a) make variance = w^2 exactly; sigma = w. Centres are integers since w even.

families.context: Two classes sat the same test and both have the same mean mark; only their standard deviations are given.
families.stem: Class A and Class B sat the same test and both classes have the same mean mark. The standard deviation of the marks of Class A is $\sigma_A = {=sa}$ and that of Class B is $\sigma_B = {=sb}$. Which class is more homogeneous in its marks?
solution: Both classes have the same mean, so we compare their standard deviations.
The set with the larger standard deviation is more dispersed; the set with the smaller standard deviation is more homogeneous.
$\sigma_A = {=sa}$ and $\sigma_B = {=sb}$, and {=small} is the smaller value.
Class {=w} has the smaller standard deviation, so it is more homogeneous.

proposed_misconceptions.label: Larger standard deviation taken as more homogeneous
proposed_misconceptions.description: Student picks the set with the larger standard deviation, forgetting that larger standard deviation means more dispersed and so less homogeneous.

families.notes: Pure comparison of two given standard deviations; options shuffled by the app. Stem differs per instance via sa, sb.

families.context: Two classes each have four students' marks with the same mean.

params.name: ssa
params.let: sum([d * d for d in pa])

params.name: ssb
params.let: sum([d * d for d in pb])

families.stem: The marks of four students in Class A are ${=m+pa[0]}, {=m+pa[1]}, {=m+pa[2]}, {=m+pa[3]}$ and the marks of four students in Class B are ${=m+pb[0]}, {=m+pb[1]}, {=m+pb[2]}, {=m+pb[3]}$. Both sets have the same mean. By calculating the standard deviations, decide which class is more homogeneous in its marks.
solution: The sum of Class A marks is {=4*m}, so its mean is {=m}; likewise the mean of Class B is {=m}.
Class A deviations from the mean: {=pa[0]}, {=pa[1]}, {=pa[2]}, {=pa[3]}. The sum of their squares is {=ssa}, so $\sigma_A^2 = \frac{{=ssa}}{4}$ and $\sigma_A \approx {=sga}$.
Class B deviations from the mean: {=pb[0]}, {=pb[1]}, {=pb[2]}, {=pb[3]}. The sum of their squares is {=ssb}, so $\sigma_B^2 = \frac{{=ssb}}{4}$ and $\sigma_B \approx {=sgb}$.
The set with the larger standard deviation is more dispersed.
Class {=w} has the smaller standard deviation, so it is more homogeneous.

proposed_misconceptions.label: Larger standard deviation taken as more homogeneous
proposed_misconceptions.description: Student picks the set with the larger standard deviation, forgetting that larger standard deviation means more dispersed and so less homogeneous.

families.notes: Deviation patterns are symmetric with distinct sums of squares (4,10,20,16,18,26,34), so sets are sorted, means equal m, and the comparison is never a tie. The population standard deviation is used, as in the book's solution.
